title: Shalva Besieges Dwaraka
story:
At noon the sky over Dwaraka turned dark, and the people looked up at a thing no one could name. It was not a cloud. It hung above their city — vast, dark as a storm, moving slowly by its own will, with ramparts and towers and gates of its own — and around it and behind it the sky filled with the shapes of an army.

Shalva had come. He had not forgotten the Yadavas: his friend Shishupala lay dead at the Rajasuya, and he himself had been driven off in defeat at Rukmini's wedding. Now he had brought his vengeance home in the form of Maya's flying city. Saubha moved over Dwaraka and opened itself, and everything it carried came down at once.

Weapons came first, in their hundreds. Then stones, and whole trees torn up by the roots and hurled down, and thunderbolts that struck the towers and split them, and serpents raining hissing out of the sky, and showers of gravel that rattled on the roofs like hail. The famous gardens and pleasure grounds of Dwaraka, where the city walked in the evenings, were shredded. The gates were shattered, the walls dented, the palaces and high terraces cracked and smoking. The golden city by the sea was being pounded from above, and its people ran through the streets looking up at a doom that would not come down to fight them — only to torment them from the sky, where no arrow could reach and no wall could answer.

What shook the city was not only the ruin but the helplessness. A city can stand a siege on the ground: it can man its walls, count its enemies, and wait. It cannot easily stand a siege that hangs overhead and will not be reached — a moving mountain of iron that chose its place in the sky and opened itself again and again. There was no wall to hold and no enemy to charge; only a darkness above that went on dropping ruin.

Then a voice cut through the panic. Pradyumna, Krishna's son by Rukmini, would not watch his people break. He mounted his chariot and rode out into the open, and his cry rang over the streets: "Do not fear!" The cry passed from street to street, and where it passed, panic began to turn back into purpose.

The Yadava warriors heard it and rallied. Satyaki came out, and Charudeshna, and Samba, and Akrura with his younger brothers — the chiefs of the great Yadava houses — and behind them the archers and the leaders of the chariot troops, all those who had built Dwaraka's name in war. They poured through the broken gates, horses straining, bows ready, and arrayed themselves beneath the iron city. The two hosts met in its shadow, and the clash of it rolled over the sea like thunder.

It was a battle unlike any Dwaraka had fought, for the enemy did not stand on the earth. Saubha wheeled above them, loosing weapons and magic at will, now high, now low, and the Yadavas answered from below, chasing a foe that had no fixed place. Pradyumna met the illusions of the lord of Saubha with divine weapons of his own, arrow for illusion, until the sky over the city was a snarl of light and iron, and the ground beneath it was littered with the wreckage of the morning.

And their lord was not among them. Krishna had gone to Indraprastha for the great sacrifice of his friend Yudhishthira, and the news of what hung over his city had not yet reached him. His people fought on without him, under a sky that would not stop falling.
reflection: Shalva's siege works precisely because it cannot be answered: terror from above has no face, no line of battle, no place to be met. The people's salvation is not a miracle but the courage of their own princes — Pradyumna's "Do not fear" is leadership as pure action, spoken only after he has already ridden into the open.
content_note: Siege warfare with weapons, stones, trees and serpents raining on the city; described with restraint and no graphic detail.
next_story_tease: But the omens had already reached Krishna in Indraprastha — he was on his way home.
hero_scene: The iron city Saubha hangs over Dwaraka, raining rocks and serpents and blazing weapons onto shattered gates and gardens, while below Pradyumna rides out on his chariot, one arm raised, crying "Do not fear!" to the terrified people.
